claim: Retro-2 prevents ricin toxicity through a poorly-defined mechanism of action (MOA), which involves halting retrograde vesicle transport to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The small molecule Retro-2 prevents ricin toxicity through a poorly-defined mechanism of action (MOA), which involves halting retrograde vesicle transport to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about Retro-2's known effects.

claim: CRISPRi genetic interaction analysis revealed Retro-2 activity resembles disruption of the transmembrane domain recognition complex (TRC) pathway.
source: CRISPRi genetic interaction analysis revealed Retro-2 activity resembles disruption of the transmembrane domain recognition complex (TRC) pathway, which mediates post-translational ER-targeting and insertion of tail-anchored (TA) proteins, including SNAREs required for retrograde transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPRi screening experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The TRC pathway mediates post-translational ER-targeting and insertion of tail-anchored (TA) proteins, including SNAREs required for retrograde transport.
source: CRISPRi genetic interaction analysis revealed Retro-2 activity resembles disruption of the transmembrane domain recognition complex (TRC) pathway, which mediates post-translational ER-targeting and insertion of tail-anchored (TA) proteins, including SNAREs required for retrograde transport.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the TRC pathway function.

claim: Cell-based and in vitro assays show that Retro-2 blocks delivery of newly-synthesized TA-proteins to the ER-targeting factor ASNA1 (TRC40).
source: Cell-based and in vitro assays show that Retro-2 blocks delivery of newly-synthesized TA-proteins to the ER-targeting factor ASNA1 (TRC40).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental assays described in the manuscript including fluorescent reporter assays and biochemical reconstitution experiments.

claim: An ASNA1 point mutant identified using CRISPR-mediated mutagenesis abolishes both the cytoprotective effect of Retro-2 against ricin and its inhibitory effect on ASNA1-mediated ER-targeting.
source: An ASNA1 point mutant identified using CRISPR-mediated mutagenesis abolishes both the cytoprotective effect of Retro-2 against ricin and its inhibitory effect on ASNA1-mediated ER-targeting.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR-X mutagenesis experiments and subsequent functional validation assays.

claim: Ricin evades lysosomal destruction by being sorted into early endosome-derived vesicles destined for fusion with the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: The plant toxin ricin, however, evades this fate by being sorted into early endosome-derived vesicles destined for fusion with the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ricin trafficking cited from previous literature.

claim: Following retrograde transport from the Golgi to the ER, ricin retrotranslocates into the cytosol where it catalytically disables ribosomes, halting translation and killing the cell.
source: Following further retrograde transport from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), ricin retrotranslocates into the cytosol where it catalytically disables ribosomes, halting translation and killing the cell (Crispin et al., 2009; Bassik et al., 2013; Sandvig and van Deurs, 2005; Lord et al., 2003; Johannes and Popoff, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ricin's mechanism of toxicity, supported by multiple citations.

claim: A high-throughput screen of small molecules first identified Retro-2 as an inhibitor of ricin and Shiga-like toxins that halts their retrograde progression to the ER by trapping them in the early endosome.
source: A high-throughput screen of small molecules first identified Retro-2 as an inhibitor of ricin and Shiga-like toxins that halts their retrograde progression to the ER by trapping them in the early endosome (Stechmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature (Stechmann et al., 2010).

claim: Retro-2 was able to rescue mice from lethal doses of ricin and was tolerated at high doses.
source: Remarkably, Retro-2 was able to rescue mice from lethal doses of ricin and was tolerated at high doses.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies, implicitly citing Stechmann et al., 2010.

claim: Retro-2 and its analogs can interfere with infection of papillomaviruses (such as HPV16) and polyomaviruses (such as JCPyV, BKPyV, and simian virus 40).
source: Subsequent studies of the bioactive cyclic derivative of Retro-2 (hereafter Retro-2) (Park et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2013) and its analogs have also revealed the ability of these compounds to interfere with infection of papillomaviruses (such as HPV16) (Lipovsky et al., 2013) and polyomaviruses (such as JCPyV, BKPyV, and simian virus 40) (Nelson et al., 2013), which are known to rely on retrograde transport during infection.
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Papillomaviruses and polyomaviruses are known to rely on retrograde transport during infection.
source: Subsequent studies of the bioactive cyclic derivative of Retro-2 (hereafter Retro-2) (Park et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2013) and its analogs have also revealed the ability of these compounds to interfere with infection of papillomaviruses (such as HPV16) (Lipovsky et al., 2013) and polyomaviruses (such as JCPyV, BKPyV, and simian virus 40) (Nelson et al., 2013), which are known to rely on retrograde transport during infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about viral infection mechanisms.

claim: Retro-2 treatment affects the localization of Syntaxin 5 (STX5) and less acutely Syntaxin 6.
source: While the mechanism of action (MOA) of Retro-2 is not well understood, Retro-2 has been shown to affect the localization of Syntaxin 5 (STX5) and less acutely Syntaxin 6 (Stechmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by Stechmann et al., 2010.

claim: STX5 is a target-SNARE required for fusion of retrograde vesicles with the TGN.
source: STX5 – a target-SNARE – is required for fusion of retrograde vesicles with the TGN, and knockdown of its expression is sufficient to trap ricin in the early endosome (Amessou et al., 2007; Dascher and Balch, 1996; Suga et al., 2005; Norlin et al., 2016; Bennett et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Knockdown of STX5 expression is sufficient to trap ricin in the early endosome.
source: STX5 – a target-SNARE – is required for fusion of retrograde vesicles with the TGN, and knockdown of its expression is sufficient to trap ricin in the early endosome (Amessou et al., 2007; Dascher and Balch, 1996; Suga et al., 2005; Norlin et al., 2016; Bennett et al., 1993).
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Most SNAREs like STX5 are tail-anchored (TA) proteins with a single, C-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) that are post-translationally targeted to the ER for insertion by the transmembrane domain recognition complex (TRC) pathway.
source: Most SNAREs like STX5 are tail-anchored (TA) proteins – a class of membrane proteins with a single, C-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) that are post-translationally targeted to the ER for insertion by the transmembrane domain recognition complex (TRC) pathway (Hegde and Keenan, 2011; Denic, 2012; Cho et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TA protein biogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: Previous genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 deletion screens identified STX5 and ASNA1 among the top hits that confer resistance to ricin.
source: Notably, our previous genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 deletions screens have identified STX5 and its ER targeting factor, ASNA1 (also known as TRC40) among the top hits that confer resistance to ricin (Morgens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: The genes whose genetic profile correlated most strongly with the profile of Retro-2 were WRB, STX5, SGTA, and GET4.
source: The genes whose genetic profile correlated most strongly with the profile of Retro-2 were WRB, STX5, SGTA, and GET4 (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F; Figure 1—source datas 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by the paired-gene CRISPRi screen data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The genetic profiles of ASNA1 and CAMLG were uninformative and did not correlate with Retro-2.
source: Notably, the genetic profiles of ASNA1 and CAMLG were uninformative (and did not correlate with Retro-2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G); this is likely because the guides targeting these genes individually had extremely protective ricin phenotypes (independent of the second guide), suggesting either that their phenotypes cannot be modified or the variance is outside the dynamic range of this experiment.
evidence: This is supported by the screening data and explained by the authors' interpretation.

claim: Guides targeting ASNA1 and CAMLG individually had extremely protective ricin phenotypes independent of the second guide.
source: Notably, the genetic profiles of ASNA1 and CAMLG were uninformative (and did not correlate with Retro-2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G); this is likely because the guides targeting these genes individually had extremely protective ricin phenotypes (independent of the second guide), suggesting either that their phenotypes cannot be modified or the variance is outside the dynamic range of this experiment.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the screening data.

claim: Pre-treatment of wild-type cells with either Retro-2 or DHQZ36.1 resulted in a comparable RFP:GFP ratio decrease that was not further aggravated by the additional absence of ASNA1.
source: Strikingly, pre-treatment of wild-type cells with either Retro-2 or a hyperactive analog of Retro-2, DHQZ36.1 (Craig et al., 2017), resulted in a comparable RFP:GFP ratio decrease that was not further aggravated by the additional absence of ASNA1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with an inactive analog of Retro-2, DHQZ5, resulted in no significant reporter changes.
source: In contrast, we detected no significant reporter changes when we treated cells with an inactive analog of Retro-2, DHQZ5 (Carney et al., 2014)(Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or when we used a control reporter lacking the TMD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: A control reporter lacking the TMD showed no significant changes upon Retro-2 treatment.
source: In contrast, we detected no significant reporter changes when we treated cells with an inactive analog of Retro-2, DHQZ5 (Carney et al., 2014)(Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or when we used a control reporter lacking the TMD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Recognition of SEC61B by ASNA1 can be abolished by appending a C-terminal sequence, leading to preferential TMD engagement by the signal recognition particle (SRP) on the ribosome.
source: Previous in vitro work with SEC61Β showed that recognition by ASNA1 can be abolished by appending a C-terminal sequence, leading to preferential TMD engagement by the signal recognition particle (SRP) on the ribosome (Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous in vitro work.

claim: The co-translational reporter GFP-2A-RFP-SEC61BTMD-BFP was no longer destabilized in ASNA1KO cells.
source: To switch the ER targeting specificity of SEC61B TMD in cells by a similar approach, we fused the blue fluorescent protein (BFP) to the C-terminus of GFP-RFP-SEC61BTMD (GFP-2A-RFP-SEC61BTMD-BFP) and confirmed that the resulting co-translational reporter was no longer destabilized in ASNA1KO cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The co-translational reporter modification conferred reporter resistance to DHQZ36.1 in both wildtype and ASNA1KO cells.
source: Consistent with our model, this modification also conferred reporter resistance to DHQZ36.1 in both wildtype and ASNA1KO cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ASNA1 knockdown conferred resistance to ricin toxicity that was comparable to that caused by Retro-2.
source: First, we established HeLa cells expressing either shRNAs targeting ASNA1 or scrambled negative control shRNAs and demonstrated that only the former knockdown conferred resistance to ricin toxicity that was comparable to that caused by Retro-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy revealed a reduction in STX5 fluorescence density at the Golgi upon Retro-2-treatment of control cells that was comparable to that observed in untreated ASNA1 knockdown cells.
source: Immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy revealed a reduction in STX5 fluorescence density at the Golgi upon Retro-2-treatment of control cells that was comparable to that observed in untreated ASNA1 knockdown cells (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Combining Retro-2 treatment with ASNA1 knockdown resulted in a more severe loss of STX5 at the Golgi.
source: Combining Retro-2 treatment with ASNA1 knockdown resulted in a more severe loss of STX5 at the Golgi (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The hyperactive Retro-2 analog DHQZ36.1 caused a severe loss of Golgi STX5 similar to Retro-2-treated ASNA1 knockdown cells.
source: We also monitored the activity of the hyperactive Retro-2 analog DHQZ36.1 (Craig et al., 2017) and observed that it caused a severe loss of Golgi STX5 similar to Retro-2-treated ASNA1 knockdown cells (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The most common ASNA1 mutation in both replicates of the CRISPR-X screen was C460T, which results in an alanine to valine coding change (A149V).
source: The most common ASNA1 mutation in both replicates, C460T, results in an alanine to valine coding change (A149V), and we obtained two lines of cell-based evidence that it represents a bona fide resistance allele (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the CRISPR-X mutagenesis and sequencing data.

claim: The A149V mutation conferred resistance to the toxicity of DHQZ36.1, whereas a synonymous control mutation (C461T; A149A) did not.
source: Using both mixed pools of edited cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and clonally selected homozygous mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B), we found that the A149V mutation conferred resistance to the toxicity of DHQZ36.1, whereas a synonymous control mutation (C461T; A149A) did not (Figure 4—figure supplements 1C and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The A149V ASNA1 mutation conferred resistance to the protective activity of Retro-2 against ricin whereas the synonymous mutation had little effect.
source: More critically, the A149V ASNA1 mutation also conferred resistance to the protective activity of Retro-2 against ricin whereas the synonymous mutation had little effect (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplements 1D and 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4D and supplementary figures.

claim: Cells expressing ASNA1 A149V have an approximately ten times higher half maximal effective concentration (EC50) for both Retro-2 and DHQZ36.1 than wildtype and ASNA1 A149A cells.
source: However, analysis of the reporter dose response revealed that cells expressing ASNA1 A149V have an approximately ten times higher half maximal effective concentration (EC50) for both Retro-2 and DHQZ36.1 than wildtype and ASNA1 A149A cells (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DHQZ36.1 caused a small decrease in the formation of the crosslinked ASNA1×STX5TMD adduct.
source: DHQZ36.1 caused a small decrease in the formation of the crosslinked ASNA1×STX5TMD adduct (Figure 5B,C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro crosslinking data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: DHQZ5, the inactive Retro-2 analog, behaved like the vehicle control in the crosslinking assay.
source: In contrast, DHQZ5, the inactive Retro-2 analog (Carney et al., 2014), behaved like the vehicle control.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro crosslinking data.

claim: DHQZ36.1 treatment reduced ASNA1~SEC61B complex formation.
source: We also repeated our crosslinking analysis on SEC61Β, a classic ASNA1 substrate in vitro, and found DHQZ36.1 treatment also reduced ASNA1~SEC61B complex formation. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro crosslinking data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The presence of DHQZ36.1 but not its biologically inactive derivative DHQZ5 obstructed STX5TMD and SEC61B delivery to ASNA1 in the purified component assay.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the presence of DHQZ36.1 but not its biologically inactive derivative DHQZ5 (Carney et al., 2014) obstructed STX5TMD, as well as SEC61Β, delivery to ASNA1 under these conditions (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro transfer assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: While SEC61B was transferred efficiently to ASNA1 A143V, inhibition of ASNA1×TA protein adducts by addition of DHQZ36.1 was no longer observed.
source: While SEC61B was transferred efficiently to ASNA1 A143V, we no longer observed inhibition of ASNA1×TA protein adducts by addition of DHQZ36.1 (Figure 5F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro transfer assay data with the mutant ASNA1 shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both Retro-2 treatment and ASNA1 knockout reduce insulin content and induce ER stress in isolated mouse islet cells.
source: Second, both Retro-2 treatment and ASNA1 knockout reduce insulin content and induce ER stress in isolated mouse islet cells (Norlin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by Norlin et al., 2016.

claim: Mapping of the top ASNA1 resistance allele onto the structure of yeast Get3 revealed its location within Helix 6.
source: Intriguingly, mapping of our top ASNA1 resistance allele onto the structure of yeast Get3 revealed its location within Helix 6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Helix 6 structural elements appear to have an allosteric role in stimulating ATPase activity.
source: These structural elements appear to have an allosteric role in stimulating ATPase activity (Mateja et al., 2009) and warrant an enzymatic analysis of the effects of Retro-2 on ASNA1 during the pre-targeting step.
evidence: This is cited from previous structural work by Mateja et al., 2009.

claim: Retro-2 has protective activity against human cytomegalovirus, filoviruses such as Marburg and Ebola, Vaccinia, chlamydia, leishmania, and enteroviruses.
source: However, retrograde trafficking has not been implicated in the life cycles of many Retro-2-sensitive viruses and endocytic pathogens such as human cytomegalovirus (Cruz et al., 2017), filoviruses such as Marburg and Ebola (Shtanko et al., 2018), Vaccinia (Sivan et al., 2016), chlamydia (Herweg et al., 2016), leishmania (Craig et al., 2017), and enteroviruses (Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Retrograde trafficking has not been implicated in the life cycles of many Retro-2-sensitive viruses and endocytic pathogens.
source: However, retrograde trafficking has not been implicated in the life cycles of many Retro-2-sensitive viruses and endocytic pathogens such as human cytomegalovirus (Cruz et al., 2017), filoviruses such as Marburg and Ebola (Shtanko et al., 2018), Vaccinia (Sivan et al., 2016), chlamydia (Herweg et al., 2016), leishmania (Craig et al., 2017), and enteroviruses (Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on the cited literature.

claim: Herpes simplex virus 1, Epstein-Barr, and human papillomavirus 6 and 8 are known to depend on the TRC pathway.
source: In addition, our work provides impetus to examine the efficacy of Retro-2 against viruses such as Herpes simplex virus 1 (Ott et al., 2016), Epstein-Barr (Horst et al., 2011), and human papillomavirus 6 and 8 (Sullivan and Coscoy, 2010), which are known to depend on the TRC pathway.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: In the paired-gene CRISPRi strategy, the top four genes were all members of the TRC pathway.
source: In our paired-gene CRISPRi strategy, the top four genes were all members of the TRC pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the paired-gene CRISPRi screen.

claim: The fifth gene in the paired-gene CRISPRi screen was SRP54, a factor that plays an analogous role to ASNA1 in the co-translational ER protein targeting pathway.
source: The fifth gene was SRP54, a factor that plays an analogous role to ASNA1 in the co-translational ER protein targeting pathway (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the paired-gene CRISPRi screen.

claim: There is no evidence that Retro-2 affects co-translational ER protein targeting.
source: We have found no evidence, however, that Retro-2 affects co-translational ER protein targeting (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Very low levels of interaction between TA proteins and SRP54 have been detected in vitro.
source: While very low levels of interaction between TA proteins and SRP54 have been detected in vitro (Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007), a wealth of evidence demonstrates that the SRP pathway does not mediate TA protein insertion under these conditions (Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007; Kutay et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited from previous in vitro work.

claim: The SRP pathway does not mediate TA protein insertion under normal conditions.
source: While very low levels of interaction between TA proteins and SRP54 have been detected in vitro (Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007), a wealth of evidence demonstrates that the SRP pathway does not mediate TA protein insertion under these conditions (Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007; Kutay et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: SRP54 is capable of efficiently recognizing a TA protein TMD sequence when the latter is artificially presented to it during protein translation by the ribosome.
source: Nonetheless, SRP54 is capable of efficiently recognizing a TA protein TMD sequence when the latter is artificially presented to it during protein translation by the ribosome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SRP54 function.

claim: Retro-2 directly inhibits ASNA1, leading to inefficient ER targeting of TRC pathway clients such as STX5, which ultimately prevents retrograde trafficking of ricin and protects the cell.
source: Collectively, these findings support a model in which Retro-2 directly inhibits ASNA1, leading to inefficient ER targeting of TRC pathway clients such as STX5, which ultimately prevents retrograde trafficking of ricin and protects the cell.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed model based on their collective findings.

claim: This study defines the first known chemical inhibitor of the TRC pathway.
source: Finally, this study defines the first known chemical inhibitor of the TRC pathway and could be an impetus for pharmaceutical efforts to drug this pathway as a therapy against diverse viruses and pathogens.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: ASNA1 is an essential gene for cell growth in CRISPR/Cas9 screens in K562.
source: Along with our previous result that ASNA1 is an essential gene for cell growth in CRISPR/Cas9 screens in K562 (Morgens et al., 2017), these observations suggested that the toxicity of Retro-2 and DHQZ36.1 may be mediated by strong inhibition of ASNA1.
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: ASNA1 knockdown sensitizes cells to growth inhibition by high concentrations of Retro-2 even in the absence of ricin.
source: Second, we noted that ASNA1 knockdown sensitizes cells to growth inhibition by high concentrations of Retro-2 even in the absence of ricin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and that high doses of DHQZ36.1 are toxic to cell growth even in wildtype cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High doses of DHQZ36.1 are toxic to cell growth even in wildtype cells.
source: Second, we noted that ASNA1 knockdown sensitizes cells to growth inhibition by high concentrations of Retro-2 even in the absence of ricin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and that high doses of DHQZ36.1 are toxic to cell growth even in wildtype cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TA proteins that are not efficiently delivered to ASNA1 are channeled to degradation.
source: To test whether Retro-2 disrupts the biogenesis of TRC pathway substrates, we exploited the molecular triage decision that channels newly-synthesized TA proteins that are not efficiently delivered to ASNA1 to degradation (Shao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by Shao et al., 2017.

claim: ASNA1KO HEK293T cells showed significantly lower RFP:GFP ratio following dox treatment, confirming the dependence of the reporter on the TRC pathway.
source: As expected, we observed by flow cytometry significantly lower RFP: GFP ratio in the ASNA1KO cells following dox treatment, confirming the dependence of the reporter on the TRC pathway (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Formation of ASNA1-TA protein complexes is preceded by TMD capture by SGTA, the most upstream factor in the TRC pathway.
source: Formation of ASNA1-TA protein complexes is preceded by TMD capture by SGTA, the most upstream factor in the TRC pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the TRC pathway.

claim: TA proteins are transferred from SGTA to ASNA1 by a mechanism mediated by the BAG6 complex (comprising BAG6, GET4, and UBL4A).
source: Following this pre-targeting step, TA proteins are transferred from SGTA to ASNA1 by a mechanism mediated by the BAG6 complex (comprising BAG6, GET4, and UBL4A) (Shao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by Shao et al., 2017.

claim: The zebrafish ASNA1 A143V mutation corresponds to the human ASNA1 A149V mutation that confers Retro-2 resistance.
source: Finally, we analyzed the effect of the zebrafish ASNA1 A143V mutation, which corresponds to the human ASNA1 A149V mutation that confers Retro-2 resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Retro-2 and its analogs target the TRC pathway.
source: Here, we have demonstrated that Retro-2 and its hyperactive analog, DHQZ36.1, target the TRC pathway.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: DHQZ36.1 inhibits transfer of TA proteins from SGTA to ASNA1 in a biochemically defined system.
source: First, DHQZ36.1 inhibits transfer of TA proteins from SGTA to ASNA1 in a biochemically defined system (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro transfer assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Retro-2 and DHQZ36.1 prevent the insertion of newly-synthesized TA protein reporters.
source: Second, Retro-2 and DHQZ36.1 prevent the insertion of newly-synthesized TA protein reporters (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: An ASNA1 mutation prevents four distinct forms of Retro-2/DHQZ36.1 activity: cytoprotection against ricin, inhibition of growth, ASNA1 substrate destabilization associated with ER targeting disruption, and inhibition of assisted substrate transfer from SGTA to ASNA1.
source: Third, an ASNA1 mutation prevents four distinct forms of Retro-2/DHQZ36.1 activity: cytoprotection against ricin, inhibition of growth, ASNA1 substrate destabilization associated with ER targeting disruption, and inhibition of assisted substrate transfer from SGTA to ASNA1.
evidence: This is a summary of the multiple experimental results with the ASNA1 A149V mutant.

claim: Retro-2 treatment interferes with STX5 localization to the Golgi.
source: First, Retro-2 treatment interferes with STX5 localization to the Golgi (Stechmann et al., 2010), which can now be understood as an expected consequence of ASNA1 inhibition.
evidence: This is cited from previous work and reinterpreted in light of the current findings.

claim: The ability of Retro-2 to inhibit the TRC pathway and disrupt STX5 may be sufficient to explain its protective activity against ricin and other toxins and viruses that rely on retrograde trafficking.
source: The ability of Retro-2 to inhibit the TRC pathway and disrupt STX5 may be sufficient to explain its protective activity against ricin and other toxins and viruses that similarly rely on retrograde trafficking (Nelson et al., 2013; Lipovsky et al., 2013; Maru et al., 2017; Nonnenmacher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their findings and cited literature.
